newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industry fights alcohol ad limits.
newsitem.headline: German industry fights alcohol ad limits.

text.p: In the face of sinking alcohol consumption in Germany, the advertising and beverage industries on Tuesday stepped up their campaign to defeat proposed restrictions on advertising for beer, wine and liquor.

"There is no reason to further limit freedom of speech and freedom to conduct business, which are basic rights in a free market," Germany's central advertising group (ZAW) and alcohol industry representatives said in a joint statement.

Several state premiers and national officials, including Health Minister Horst Seehofer, have called for limits on alcohol advertising in recent weeks in order to decrease drinking, particularly among young people.

The ZAW and alcohol industry groups said, however, that alcohol consumption has been steadily decreasing for several years, dropping by nearly 16 litres per year per person to 160.8 litres between 1987 and 1996.

They added that advertising expenditures in the alcohol industry more than doubled during the same period, jumping to 1.2 billion marks ($653.4 million) from 500 million marks per year as a result of more intense competition in a shrinking market.

Industry representatives denied a link between drinking among youths and ads during television sports programming, saying that ratings from the GfK research firm indicate only 2.8 percent of 14 to 19 year olds watch TV sports.
"The great majority of (TV sports) viewers are over 40 and comprise the target group of alcoholic drink manufacturers," the statement said.
The ZAW also rejected the claim by bill supporters that Germany tops the list of per capita alcohol consumption in Europe, saying its rank was around eighth place.
The industries pointed to what they called the failure of limits of ads for alcohol in Norway, Finland and Sweden, where they said drinking continued to increase despite fewer ads.
The groups said they also objected to voluntary, industry-imposed guidelines.
"Such policies ultimately have the same effect of manipulating the freedom to communicate in the market," they said.
Supporters of the limits, including the German Centre Against Addiction (DHS), blasted the data in the statement, saying they had manipulated published data to support their position.

"The DHS can understand that the associations of the alcohol and advertising industries are nervous about the public debate over their 1.2 billion mark a year business," the DHS said in a statement, referring to spending on alcohol ads.
"(But) the DHS strongly criticises the claims of the ZAW and note that many of their comparisons are either incorrect or invalid," it said.
